marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q001.takeaway: Hyoid bone supports the larynx but is not a laryngeal cartilage/skeleton element.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q001.displayText:
The structure marked A is the hyoid bone, which is not part of the laryngeal skeleton. The marked structures are hyoid bone, thyroid cartilage, epiglottis, and cricoid cartilage.

The laryngeal skeleton is formed by cartilages connected by ligaments and fibrous membranes. Thyroid, cricoid, and most of the arytenoid cartilages are hyaline. Corniculate, cuneiform, triticeal, epiglottic cartilages and the apices of the arytenoids are elastic.
emphasis: not part of the laryngeal skeleton

rationales.b: Thyroid cartilage is a major component of laryngeal skeleton, unlike hyoid bone.
rationales.c: Epiglottis is a laryngeal cartilage attached to hyoid and thyroid, not the exception.
rationales.d: Cricoid cartilage forms laryngeal framework; hyoid bone itself is not part of skeleton.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q003.takeaway: Cricoid is the only complete laryngeal cartilaginous ring.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q003.displayText:
Cricoid cartilage forms a complete ring around the airway and is the only laryngeal cartilage to do so.

Clinical significance: in Sellick manoeuvre, cricoid pressure is applied to occlude the esophagus without occluding the airway, helping prevent regurgitation of gastric contents during rapid induction. The cricoid is also the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.

rationales.a: Thyroid cartilage is an open posterior lamina and does not form a complete ring.
rationales.c: Cuneiform cartilage is a small paired support, not a ring.
rationales.d: Epiglottis is a leaf-shaped elastic cartilage, not a complete ring.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q005.takeaway: Cricothyroid membrane is intrinsic, not an external laryngeal membrane.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q005.displayText:
The cricothyroid ligament/membrane is an intrinsic laryngeal membrane rather than an external laryngeal membrane.

The cricothyroid ligament lies between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages and has right and left lateral parts (conus elasticus) and a thickened median or anterior cricothyroid ligament.

Extrinsic ligaments and membranes include the thyrohyoid membrane, hyoepiglottic ligament, and cricotracheal ligament. Intrinsic membranes include the quadrangular membrane, cricothyroid membrane, and thyroepiglottic ligament.

rationales.b: Thyrohyoid membrane is extrinsic, connecting larynx to hyoid.
rationales.c: Cricotracheal membrane is extrinsic connection between cricoid and trachea.
rationales.d: Hyoepiglottic ligament is extrinsic; cricothyroid membrane is intrinsic.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q006.takeaway: Rima glottidis is the opening between true vocal folds.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q006.displayText:
Rima glottidis is the aperture between the vocal folds.

The upper laryngeal cavity extends from the laryngeal inlet to the vestibular folds; the vestibule lies between these. The middle part extends from rima vestibuli to rima glottidis. The ventricle lies between the vestibular and vocal folds, while the saccule is a pouch from the anterior end of the ventricle. The lower or infraglottic cavity extends from the vocal cords to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

The larynx is generally lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, except the vocal folds, lingual surface of the epiglottis, and upper part of the aryepiglottic folds, which are lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

rationales.a: The laryngeal vestibule extends from inlet to vestibular folds; the ventricle lies between false and true folds.
rationales.b: True vocal folds are lined by stratified squamous epithelium because of vibration, not respiratory pseudostratified ciliated epithelium.
rationales.d: Saccule arises anteriorly from laryngeal ventricle; it is not the ventricle itself.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q007.takeaway: Laryngocele arises from saccule (label A) and expands during raised laryngeal pressure.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q007.displayText:
The scenario is suggestive of a laryngocele. The defect is in the saccule, represented by region A in the source diagram. The other labelled structures are B: ventricle, C: vestibular ligament, and D: vocal ligament.

The saccule ascends forward from the anterior end of the ventricle between the vestibular fold and thyroid cartilage. It is conical and contains many mucous glands whose secretions lubricate the vocal cords.

Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling caused by dilatation of the saccule and is associated with activities that raise transglottic pressure, such as trumpet playing, glass blowing, or weight lifting. It may be internal, external, or combined. External laryngocele presents as a reducible neck swelling that enlarges with coughing or Valsalva.

rationales.a: Label C is vestibular ligament rather than saccule.
rationales.b: Label D marks vocal ligament, not the saccular pouch.
rationales.d: Label B is ventricle; the saccule ascends from its anterior end at A.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q008.takeaway: Vestibular ligament is the thickened lower edge of quadrangular membrane.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q008.displayText:
The vestibular ligament is enclosed within the false vocal cords. The lower free margin of the quadrangular membrane is thickened to form the vestibular ligament.

False vocal cords are formed by vestibular folds and contain the vestibular ligament, a few fibres of thyroarytenoideus, and mucous glands. True vocal cords extend from the thyroid angle to the vocal processes of the arytenoids and contain the vocal ligament and subepithelial connective tissue. The upper free margin of the cricovocal ligament/cricothyroid membrane/conus elasticus is thickened to form the vocal ligament.
emphasis: lower free margin of the quadrangular membrane

rationales.a: cricothyroid ligament/membrane is the upper thickened edge of conus elasticus, not lower quadrangular membrane.
rationales.c: Upper free edge of quadrangular membrane forms aryepiglottic ligament, not vestibular ligament.
rationales.d: Conus elasticus is lower laryngeal membrane; its upper edge forms vocal ligament.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q010.takeaway: Thyroarytenoid relaxes vocal cords; posterior cricoarytenoid alone abducts them.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q010.displayText: The image shows an endoscopic view of the vocal cords. Thyroarytenoid does not abduct the vocal cords; it relaxes the vocal cords and helps close the rima glottidis.

rationales.b: Lateral cricoarytenoid adducts vocal folds, so this is a true statement.
rationales.c: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor; this is true.
rationales.d: Cricothyroid tenses vocal cord; this is true. The incorrect statement is thyroarytenoid causes abduction.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q011.takeaway: Posterior cricoarytenoid (label 3) is the sole vocal-fold abductor.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q011.displayText:
The scenario is unilateral vocal-cord palsy due to involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The posterior cricoarytenoid, marked 3, is paralyzed; it is the abductor of the vocal cord.

In the source figure: 1 is lateral cricoarytenoid, which closes the ligamentous part of the rima glottidis; 2 is transverse arytenoid, which closes the intercartilaginous part; 3 is posterior cricoarytenoid; and 4 is cricothyroid, the tensor of the vocal cord.

rationales.a: Lateral cricoarytenoid closes ligamentous rima glottidis and is an adductor.
rationales.b: Transverse arytenoid closes intercartilaginous rima, not the sole abductor.
rationales.d: Label 4 is not the posterior cricoarytenoid; the source marks abductor as 3.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q012.takeaway: Sensory laryngeal innervation changes at vocal cords: internal superior laryngeal above, recurrent below.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q012.displayText:
Sensory innervation above the level of the vocal cords is through the internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Below the vocal cords it is through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. At the level of the cords, both internal and recurrent laryngeal nerves contribute.

All intrinsic muscles of the larynx are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
emphasis: above the level of the vocal cords
At the level of the cords

rationales.b: Above cords, internal laryngeal branch of superior laryngeal nerve supplies sensation; recurrent laryngeal does not supply that level.
rationales.c: Below cords, sensation travels through recurrent laryngeal, not internal laryngeal.
rationales.d: External laryngeal is predominantly motor to cricothyroid, not below-cord sensory supply.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q013.takeaway: External laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid; recurrent laryngeal supplies other intrinsic muscles.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q013.displayText:
The false statement is that the external laryngeal nerve supplies all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. In fact, the external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

The larynx contains three paired cartilages (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) and three unpaired cartilages (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid). Triticeal cartilage may also be present as a variable small cartilage within the lateral thyrohyoid membrane.

rationales.a: The larynx has nine cartilages: three paired and three unpaired, so this is true.
rationales.b: Larynx extends roughly C3–C6, a true relation.
rationales.d: Cricothyroid is a tensor, a true statement; external laryngeal nerve supplies it, so option C is false.

marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q014.takeaway: External laryngeal nerve injury can paralyze cricothyroid and lower pitch.
marrow__ANAT_CH34_Q014.displayText:
The nerve closely related to the superior thyroid artery is the external laryngeal nerve. Injury causes paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle, the principal tensor of the vocal cord, leading to decreased pitch of voice.

The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane at a higher level and is therefore not the nerve described. Other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

rationales.a: Internal laryngeal nerve supplies supraglottic sensation, not the nerve coursing alongside superior thyroid artery described.
rationales.b: Recurrent laryngeal nerve provides below-cord sensation and intrinsic motor supply, but injury to external laryngeal nerve along superior thyroid artery affects cricothyroid.
rationales.c: Lateral cricoarytenoid is recurrent-laryngeal supplied, not the specific superior thyroid artery companion. The external laryngeal nerve injury causes cricothyroid paralysis.
